name: Synvar
description: Synvar is a short-chain SNT-derived compound that temporarily rewires cross-modal sensory processing, inducing genuine synesthesia by creating transient synaptic bridges between sensory cortices. Users taste sound as distinct flavors, see music as moving color, hear color as tonal harmonics — the experience is not metaphorical but neurologically literal for the duration. Helix markets it as an 'expanded perception compound' and sells it in measured doses with their signature precision branding.
effects: Full cross-modal synesthesia — sound has taste, color has sound, touch has smell
side_effects: Nausea when exposed to discordant stimuli
Temporary difficulty distinguishing sensory modes post-use
Rare: persistent mild synesthesia lasting weeks after repeated use
Migraine-level headaches in users with certain BCI configurations
cultural_context: Synvar has a devoted following among GLMZ's creative and intellectual communities — it's considered a tool as much as a pleasure, used for creative breakthroughs, philosophical exploration, and the kind of parties where people sit in dark rooms and someone plays a single sustained chord for forty minutes. In Tier 4 corporate culture, there's a small but significant subset of executives who microdose Synvar for lateral thinking in high-stakes meetings. The drug has its own subculture with dedicated 'crosswire spaces' — venues designed to be experienced synesthetically.
story_hooks: A composer has released an album that is, according to Synvar users, a completely different and secretly superior work — she designed it specifically to be heard under synesthesia, and she refuses to confirm or deny this publicly

A Shelf street chemist has synthesized a crude Synvar analog that causes the synesthesia without an off-ramp — users get stuck in cross-modal loops, unable to process sensory input normally, and the chemist has disappeared

A Tier 4 executive keeps Synvar on his prescription and uses it in negotiations — he claims he can taste when someone is lying, and he's been right enough times that people are starting to believe him
